label: Europe
subtitle: Regional, seasonal, bread, herbs, preservation
about: This is a navigation umbrella, not one cuisine: it spans Atlantic coasts, Mediterranean shores, central plains, Alpine and Carpathian mountains, and eastern river systems. Its foodways were shaped by Roman and medieval trade, Christianity and fasting traditions, imperial borders, migration, New World crops and modern national cuisines. Representative dishes across this node include French pot-au-feu, Italian risotto, Hungarian pörkölt and Polish pierogi, but none should be treated as pan-European.
flavors: black pepper — multilingual node; representative DE schwarzer Pfeffer, FR poivre noir, IT pepe nero
parsley — representative DE Petersilie, FR persil, IT prezzemolo, PL pietruszka
bay leaf — representative FR feuille de laurier, ES laurel, IT alloro, RU лавровый лист (lavrovyy list)
garlic — representative FR ail, ES ajo, IT aglio, PL czosnek
mustard — representative FR moutarde, DE Senf, PL musztarda
caraway — representative DE Kümmel, CS kmín, PL kminek
dill — representative PL koperek, RU укроп (ukrop), DE Dill
thyme — representative FR thym, IT timo, ES tomillo
paprika — representative HU paprika, ES pimentón, DE Paprika
vinegar — representative FR vinaigre, ES vinagre, IT aceto, DE Essig
shortcuts: LOW CONFIDENCE at branch level: salt-free mixed European herb blends can replace the same combined dried herbs 1:1 by weight; salt 0 g if the label is truly salt-free.

Bouillon cubes or stock concentrates commonly contain salt plus yeast extract, vegetables, fats and flavorings; use only according to the product's stock-equivalence instructions rather than as a direct substitute for homemade stock. For salt accounting, salt_g = sodium_mg × 2.5 / 1000 for the amount used.
allergen_notes: No single allergen pattern covers Europe. Prepared bouillon, sauce powders and seasoning mixes may contain wheat, milk or soy; nut sauces may contain tree nuts; mayonnaise-style condiments contain egg; anchovy and fish-based seasonings contain fish; seafood pastes can contain shellfish; tahini-containing Mediterranean condiments contain sesame. Peanuts are not a defining traditional seasoning in these nodes but can appear in modern packaged products.
pitfalls: Do not treat Europe as having a single authentic flavor palette, pantry or prohibition list. LOW CONFIDENCE applies to any branch-level flavor inference; use the national or regional child node whenever possible. Avoid claiming that paprika, olive oil, butter, dill, garlic or caraway is universal across the continent.
sources: Alan Davidson, The Oxford Companion to Food, 3rd ed., Oxford University Press, 2014

label: Italy
subtitle: Regional pasta, rice, olive oil
about: Italy runs from the Alps and Po Valley through the Apennines to long Mediterranean coasts and the islands of Sicily and Sardinia, and its cooking remains intensely local and city-based. Greek, Roman, Arab, Norman, Spanish, Austrian and French rule and trade all left regional traces, while nineteenth- and twentieth-century migration helped create a national and global idea of Italian food. Representative dishes include risotto alla milanese, tagliatelle al ragù, spaghetti alle vongole and pasta alla Norma.
flavors: anchovy — acciuga/acciughe (acciuga/acciughe), used as a savory seasoning
nutmeg — noce moscata (noce moscata), especially northern/central
sweet_only: vanilla — vaniglia (vaniglia), used mainly in pastry and gelato
signature_ingredients: Parmigiano Reggiano — substitute: good domestic Parmesan, though flavor differs
guanciale — substitute: pancetta; bacon is smokier and less exact
00 flour — substitute: all-purpose flour for many preparations, adjusting hydration
Carnaroli or Arborio rice — substitute: another short- or medium-grain rice, though risotto texture differs
dried porcini — substitute: cremini plus a small amount of mushroom powder
fresh egg pasta sheets — substitute: quality dried lasagna sheets where appropriate
techniques: soffritto: gently sweating chopped aromatics in fat
mantecatura: emulsifying pasta or risotto with starch, fat and/or cheese
grilling and roasting with restrained seasoning
fresh or dried pasta making and boiling
shortcuts: Salt-free 'Italian seasoning' usually combines oregano, basil, thyme and rosemary; replace the same combined dried herbs 1:1 by weight, salt 0 g. It is an export convenience, not a traditional Italian pantry blend.
Jarred pesto may replace homemade pesto 1:1 by weight when pesto itself is the intended sauce; salt varies by brand, so calculate salt_g = sodium_mg × 2.5 / 1000 for the amount used.
Anchovy paste can replace finely mashed anchovy by approximately equal weight for seasoning applications; salt varies substantially, so account from the label rather than adding a fixed salt value.
allergen_notes: Pesto commonly contains milk from hard cheese and tree nuts from pine nuts or walnuts; some commercial pesto contains cashew. Anchovies and anchovy paste contain fish. Fresh pasta often contains egg, while ordinary dried semolina pasta usually contains wheat but not egg. Bouillon and packaged sauce bases may contain wheat, milk or soy. Sesame and peanuts are not defining traditional seasonings but may appear in modern products.
pitfalls: Do not put oregano, basil, garlic and red pepper into every Italian dish. Do not assume tomato sauce is universal, especially in northern dishes, and do not drown pasta in sauce: many traditional preparations depend on emulsification and modest condiment amounts. Avoid treating cream-heavy Alfredo, chicken Parmesan, spaghetti with meatballs or pepperoni pizza as normal nationwide Italian home cooking.
sources: Alberto Capatti and Massimo Montanari, Italian Cuisine: A Cultural History, Columbia University Press, 2003
Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking, Alfred A. Knopf, 1992

label: Northern Italy
subtitle: Butter, risotto, polenta, sage, cheeses
about: Northern Italy stretches from the Alps through Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Liguria and the Po Valley around cities such as Turin, Milan, Bologna, Venice and Genoa. Alpine agriculture, the rice-growing Po plain, Adriatic trade and long Austrian, French and Central European contacts shaped a cuisine with more butter, cheese, rice and polenta than the southern stereotype of Italian food suggests. Representative dishes include risotto alla milanese, bagna càuda, polenta concia and bollito misto.
flavors: garlic — aglio (aglio), important but not universal
balsamic vinegar — aceto balsamico (aceto balsamico), Emilia
sweet_only: vanilla — vaniglia (vaniglia), common in custards and pastry
signature_ingredients: Carnaroli or Vialone Nano rice — substitute: Arborio rice
polenta bramata or other coarse polenta — substitute: coarse yellow cornmeal
Taleggio or Fontina — substitute: a mild washed-rind cheese or young Gruyère depending dish
speck — substitute: prosciutto plus a small smoky element; not exact
dried porcini — substitute: cremini plus mushroom powder
fresh chestnuts or chestnut flour — substitute: packaged roasted chestnuts or no close flour substitute
techniques: risotto with gradual liquid addition and final mantecatura
stuffed fresh pasta and dumpling making
shortcuts: Jarred Ligurian pesto can replace freshly made pesto 1:1 by weight; check salt by label and count milk/tree-nut allergens.

Prepared broth concentrate can stand in for brodo when time matters; dilute to the manufacturer's stated stock strength rather than replacing stock concentrate 1:1 with finished broth. Salt is label-dependent.
Salt-free dried sage-rosemary-parsley mixtures may replace the same combined dried herbs 1:1 by weight; salt 0 g.
allergen_notes: Pesto commonly contains milk and tree nuts. Filled fresh pastas usually contain wheat and egg and often milk. Anchovy-based bagna càuda contains fish; traditional versions may also contain butter, adding milk. Commercial broth concentrates may contain wheat, milk or soy. Mostarda normally does not contain a major US allergen but packaged versions require label checking.
pitfalls: Do not automatically add tomato, oregano or chile to northern dishes. Risotto should not be treated as boiled rice with cream; its texture traditionally comes from rice starch and mantecatura, and cream is dish-specific. Do not assume olive oil is absent: Liguria and other northern areas have strong olive-oil traditions.
sources: Anna Del Conte, Gastronomy of Italy, Pavilion, revised edition 2013
Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking, Alfred A. Knopf, 1992

label: Southern & Sicilian
subtitle: Olive oil, tomato, oregano, capers
about: This node covers the Mediterranean-facing south of the Italian peninsula and Sicily, from Naples and Puglia through Calabria and across the Strait of Messina to Palermo and Catania. Greek settlement, Arab and Norman Sicily, Spanish rule, maritime trade and peasant agriculture left a cuisine rich in olive oil, vegetables, durum-wheat pasta, seafood, preserved fish, chile and sweet-sour combinations. Representative dishes include pizza napoletana, orecchiette con cime di rapa, pasta con le sarde and caponata.
flavors: wild fennel — finocchietto selvatico (finocchietto selvatico), especially Sicily
mint — menta (menta), especially Sicily and parts of the south
wine vinegar — aceto di vino (aceto di vino)
sweet_only: orange-blossom water — acqua di fiori d'arancio (acqua di fiori d'arancio), mainly pastry and festive sweets
signature_ingredients: ricotta salata — substitute: dry feta, less exact
caciocavallo — substitute: aged provolone
'nduja — substitute: spicy soft salami mixed with a little olive oil; not exact
bottarga — substitute: anchovy plus lemon zest for salinity/sea aroma; not texturally equivalent
fresh sardines — substitute: good canned sardines when the preparation allows
Sicilian durum-wheat semolina pasta shapes — substitute: another high-quality dried semolina pasta
techniques: frying vegetables and seafood in olive oil
grilling and roasting over direct heat
slow tomato-based sauces and vegetable braises
shortcuts: Anchovy paste can replace mashed anchovy by roughly equal weight in sauces; salt is brand-specific and must be counted from sodium on the label.
Salt-free dried oregano-basil-peperoncino blends can replace the same dried seasonings 1:1 by weight; salt 0 g. Avoid treating generic 'Italian seasoning' as a traditional southern blend.
Jarred tomato passata can replace sieved tomato 1:1 by weight when plain and unsalted; if salted, use label-derived salt accounting.
allergen_notes: Anchovies, sardines and bottarga contain fish. Pasta contains wheat and fresh pasta may contain egg. Sicilian pesto variants may contain tree nuts and milk; breadcrumbs add wheat. Some sweets and savory Sicilian dishes use pistachio, almond or pine nut. Commercial 'nduja, sauces and bouillon may contain milk, wheat or soy depending on producer.
pitfalls: Do not make every southern dish tomato-red or aggressively garlicky. Sicily is not interchangeable with Naples or Calabria: saffron, raisins, pine nuts, wild fennel and agrodolce combinations are especially Sicilian. Avoid treating chicken Parmesan, garlic bread or cream Alfredo as native southern staples.
sources: Mary Taylor Simeti, Pomp and Sustenance: Twenty-Five Centuries of Sicilian Food, Ecco, 1989
Katie Parla, Food of the Italian South, Clarkson Potter, 2019

label: Italian (Any)
subtitle: Garlic, basil, red sauce, cheese
about: This node deliberately represents the internationally recognized image of Italian food rather than a geographic region: pizza shops, red-sauce restaurants and diaspora kitchens made pasta, tomato sauce, garlic, basil and grated cheese global symbols of Italy. Much of this image was shaped by Italian migration to the Americas and later tourism and restaurant culture, so several famous dishes are export or Italian-American forms rather than everyday food across Italy. Representative dishes are spaghetti with meatballs, cream-style fettuccine Alfredo, pepperoni pizza and lasagna.
flavors: garlic — aglio (aglio), often exaggerated in export cooking
anchovy — acciuga (acciuga), less visible but traditional as savory seasoning
signature_ingredients: Parmigiano-style hard cheese — substitute: supermarket Parmesan
fresh mozzarella — substitute: low-moisture mozzarella for baked dishes
prosciutto — substitute: thinly sliced cured ham
pancetta — substitute: unsmoked bacon if available; ordinary bacon is smokier
Arborio rice — substitute: another short-grain rice
techniques: boiling pasta and finishing it in sauce
sautéing garlic and herbs in olive oil
shortcuts: Salt-free 'Italian seasoning' usually contains oregano, basil, thyme and rosemary; substitute 1:1 by weight for the same combined dried herbs, salt 0 g.
Jarred marinara commonly contains tomato, onion or garlic, herbs, oil and salt; substitute 1:1 by weight for another finished marinara, not for plain tomato. Count salt from the product label.

Prepared Alfredo sauce is an international shortcut usually containing dairy, cheese, starches and salt; substitute only for the export-style sauce, not traditional Roman fettuccine al burro. Use 1:1 by weight for another finished Alfredo sauce and count label salt.
allergen_notes: Commercial Alfredo contains milk and may contain wheat or soy thickeners. Pasta contains wheat and fresh pasta may contain egg. Pesto contains milk and usually tree nuts. Meatballs may contain wheat, egg and milk. Pizza dough contains wheat and cheese contains milk; processed pepperoni and jarred sauces require label checks for milk or soy.
pitfalls: This node is intentionally a cliché/export profile, so do not use it to police regional Italian authenticity. Spaghetti with meatballs is Italian-American, cream-heavy Alfredo is primarily an export form, and pepperoni pizza is a diaspora/commercial development. Avoid presenting these as universal Italian home traditions.
sources: Simone Cinotto, The Italian American Table: Food, Family, and Community in New York City, University of Illinois Press, 2013

label: French
subtitle: Stocks, herbs, butter, wine, mustard
about: France stretches from Atlantic and Channel coasts through river valleys and agricultural plains to the Alps, Pyrenees and Mediterranean Provence, with Paris historically central to restaurant and haute-cuisine culture. Court cuisine, regional peasant cooking, wine culture, colonial trade and chefs such as Carême and Escoffier shaped a cuisine that ranges from butter-and-cream Normandy to olive-oil-rich Provence. Representative dishes include boeuf bourguignon, coq au vin, ratatouille and quiche Lorraine.
flavors: bay leaf — feuille de laurier (feuille de laurier)
Dijon-style mustard — moutarde de Dijon (moutarde de Dijon)
nutmeg — noix de muscade (noix de muscade)
sweet_only: vanilla — vanille (vanille), mainly pastry and custard
orange-blossom water — eau de fleur d'oranger (eau de fleur d'oranger), mainly pastry in southern traditions
signature_ingredients: crème fraîche — substitute: sour cream loosened with heavy cream
lardons — substitute: thick-cut bacon, preferably not heavily smoked
duck confit or duck fat — substitute: roast duck plus rendered poultry fat; not exact
fromage blanc — substitute: quark or thick Greek yogurt depending use
celeriac — substitute: celery root if available; otherwise turnip plus celery is approximate
shortcuts: Salt-free bouquet garni sachets usually contain thyme, bay and parsley; replace an equivalent dried herb bundle 1:1 by weight, salt 0 g.

Salt-free herbes de Provence usually contains thyme, rosemary, savory, oregano and/or marjoram; replace the same combined dried herbs 1:1 by weight, salt 0 g. Lavender is an optional commercial addition, not a required traditional component.
Commercial demi-glace concentrate can replace another finished concentrate 1:1 by weight, but not finished stock. It is often highly salted; calculate salt from label sodium.
allergen_notes: Classical sauces can hide milk from butter, cream or milk; egg appears in hollandaise, mayonnaise and some liaison-thickened sauces; wheat appears in roux. Fish stock and anchovy-based sauces contain fish, shellfish stocks contain shellfish, and nut oils or nut-based regional sauces may contain tree nuts. Commercial bouillon and sauce concentrates may contain wheat, milk or soy.
pitfalls: Do not equate all French cooking with haute cuisine or mother sauces. Do not add cream and butter automatically to Provençal dishes, and do not add olive oil and garlic automatically to Normandy or Alsace. 'Herbes de Provence' is useful but should not become a universal French seasoning.

label: Spanish
subtitle: Olive oil, garlic, paprika, saffron
about: Spain occupies most of the Iberian Peninsula, with Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts, dry central plateaus and distinct regions including Galicia, the Basque Country, Catalonia, Valencia, Andalusia and the islands. Roman, Islamic, Jewish and Christian foodways, Atlantic and Mediterranean trade and the Columbian exchange shaped a highly regional cuisine centered on olive oil, vegetables, seafood, pork, legumes, rice and preserved foods. Representative dishes include paella valenciana, tortilla española, gazpacho and cocido.
flavors: olive oil — aceite de oliva (aceite de oliva)
paprika — pimentón (pimentón), smoked or unsmoked depending origin
sherry vinegar — vinagre de Jerez (vinagre de Jerez), especially Andalusian
wine vinegar — vinagre de vino (vinagre de vino)
sweet_only: orange-blossom water — agua de azahar (agua de azahar), mainly pastry and festive baking
signature_ingredients: bomba or Calasparra rice — substitute: another absorbent Spanish-style medium-grain rice
garrofó beans — substitute: large lima beans
Spanish cooking chorizo — substitute: another cured paprika sausage; Mexican fresh chorizo is not equivalent
jamón serrano — substitute: prosciutto
ñora peppers — substitute: ancho chile plus sweet paprika, an approximation
salt cod — substitute: home-salted fresh cod when time allows; plain fresh cod lacks the same texture
techniques: sofrito: slowly cooking aromatics in olive oil
dry rice cooking in a wide pan
slow stewing of legumes and meats
shortcuts: Jarred sofrito usually contains tomato, onion and/or garlic, olive oil and salt; replace homemade finished sofrito 1:1 by weight when texture permits. Count salt from the label.

Paella seasoning packets usually combine paprika, coloring and sometimes saffron, garlic or salt; formulas vary too much for a universal substitution. If replacing an explicitly specified mixed spice blend, use equal weight and calculate salt from label sodium.
Prepared allioli/alioli can replace another finished garlic emulsion 1:1 by weight; commercial versions often contain egg and salt, so account for both.
allergen_notes: Alioli made with egg contains egg. Romesco and related sauces may contain tree nuts and wheat from bread. Seafood broths and paellas may hide fish or shellfish. Some bouillon, seasoning packets and prepared sauces contain wheat, soy or milk. Sesame and peanuts are not core classic Spanish seasoning allergens but can appear in modern products.
pitfalls: Do not call all paprika smoked: Pimentón de la Vera is smoke-dried, while other Spanish pimentón traditions are not. Do not put seafood and chorizo into every paella; classic Valencian paella has its own meat-and-bean tradition. Saffron, cumin, rosemary and sherry vinegar are important but should not be forced into every Spanish recipe.
sources: Claudia Roden, The Food of Spain, Ecco, 2011
Penelope Casas, The Foods and Wines of Spain, Alfred A. Knopf, 1982

label: Greek
subtitle: Olive oil, lemon, oregano, herbs
about: Greece combines a mountainous Balkan mainland with long Aegean and Ionian coastlines and hundreds of inhabited islands, so local food varies markedly between pastoral interiors, ports and islands. Ancient Greek and Byzantine continuities mixed with Venetian, Ottoman and wider eastern Mediterranean exchange, while Orthodox fasting traditions encouraged extensive vegetable, legume and olive-oil cookery. Representative dishes include horiatiki salad, souvlaki, moussaka and gemista.
flavors: cinnamon — κανέλα (kanéla), including savory meat dishes
sweet_only: mastiha — μαστίχα (mastícha), mainly sweets, breads and liqueurs but not literally dessert-only
signature_ingredients: kefalotyri or kefalograviera — substitute: pecorino Romano or another firm sheep's-milk cheese
tarama — substitute: none; smoked fish roe is not equivalent
trahana — substitute: small pasta plus yogurt or cultured dairy gives only an approximation
gigantes beans — substitute: large lima beans
vine leaves — substitute: jarred grape leaves if fresh are unavailable
Greek strained yogurt — substitute: full-fat plain Greek-style yogurt
techniques: ladera: vegetables slowly cooked with generous olive oil
slow braising with onions, tomato, herbs and warm spices
shortcuts: Salt-free Greek herb blends generally center on oregano, garlic, thyme and pepper; replace the same combined dried herbs 1:1 by weight, salt 0 g. Salted blends require label calculation.
Bottled ladolemono commonly contains olive oil, lemon juice, oregano and salt; replace a finished lemon-oil dressing 1:1 by weight, then count salt from the label.
Prepared tzatziki can replace homemade tzatziki 1:1 by weight as a condiment; it usually contains yogurt, cucumber, garlic, herbs and salt.
allergen_notes: Tzatziki and many cheese-based sauces contain milk. Taramasalata contains fish and often wheat from bread; some versions use potato instead. Skordalia may contain wheat from bread or tree nuts from walnuts/almonds. Phyllo contains wheat; some pastries contain egg, tree nuts and sesame. Commercial spice blends may contain sesame even though it is not required.
pitfalls: Do not reduce Greek food to oregano, lemon and feta or assume every meat is grilled. Cinnamon and allspice in savory braises are authentic, but avoid inventing a simple 'Ottoman spice rule' for them. Moussaka is not an ancient unchanged national dish, and mastiha is not exclusively a dessert flavor.
sources: Diane Kochilas, The Glorious Foods of Greece, William Morrow, 2001
Aglaia Kremezi, The Foods of the Greek Islands, Houghton Mifflin, 2000

label: Central European
subtitle: Caraway, paprika, dill, horseradish, marjoram
about: This app node groups Germany, Austria, Czechia, Hungary and Poland across the North European plain, the Danube basin, the Alps and Carpathian approaches, with major centers including Berlin, Vienna, Prague, Budapest and Warsaw. Germanic, Slavic and Magyar traditions were repeatedly connected through the Holy Roman and Habsburg worlds, trade, Jewish communities and shifting borders, producing overlapping traditions of breads, dumplings, pork, cabbage, souring, paprika and preserved foods. Representative dishes include Wiener Schnitzel, Czech svíčková, Hungarian pörkölt and Polish pierogi.
flavors: caraway — DE Kümmel (Kümmel), CS kmín (kmín), HU kömény (kömény), PL kminek (kminek)
marjoram — DE Majoran (Majoran), CS majoránka (majoránka), HU majoránna (majoránna), PL majeranek (majeranek)
paprika — DE Paprika (Paprika), HU paprika (paprika), especially Hungarian
dill — DE Dill (Dill), CS kopr (kopr), HU kapor (kapor), PL koperek (koperek)
horseradish — DE Meerrettich (Meerrettich), CS křen (křen), HU torma (torma), PL chrzan (chrzan)
mustard — DE Senf (Senf), CS hořčice (hořčice), HU mustár (mustár), PL musztarda (musztarda)
garlic — DE Knoblauch (Knoblauch), CS česnek (česnek), HU fokhagyma (fokhagyma), PL czosnek (czosnek)
parsley — DE Petersilie (Petersilie), CS petržel (petržel), HU petrezselyem (petrezselyem), PL pietruszka (pietruszka)
bay leaf — DE Lorbeerblatt (Lorbeerblatt), CS bobkový list (bobkový list), HU babérlevél (babérlevél), PL liść laurowy (liść laurowy)
juniper — DE Wacholder (Wacholder), CS jalovec (jalovec), PL jałowiec (jałowiec)
black pepper — DE schwarzer Pfeffer, CS černý pepř, HU fekete bors, PL pieprz czarny
sweet_only: vanilla sugar — DE Vanillezucker, CS vanilkový cukr, HU vaníliás cukor, PL cukier waniliowy; mainly baking and sweets
signature_ingredients: quark/tvaroh/túró/twaróg fresh curd cheese — substitute: farmer cheese or well-drained cottage cheese
Hungarian wax peppers — substitute: banana peppers plus a hotter chile as needed
sour rye starter for żur/żurek — substitute: homemade rye-flour ferment; no close instant substitute
Central European smoked sausages — substitute: kielbasa or another moderately smoked pork sausage appropriate to the dish
dried porcini — substitute: cremini plus mushroom powder
bread or potato dumplings — substitute: store-bought spaetzle only when the dish can tolerate a different texture
shortcuts: LOW CONFIDENCE for this merged node: salt-free caraway-marjoram-paprika blends can replace the same combined dried spices 1:1 by weight; salt 0 g.

Commercial goulash seasoning usually contains paprika, caraway, marjoram, garlic/onion and often salt; substitute only for another specified mixed seasoning at equal weight. Count salt from label sodium.
Prepared horseradish can replace freshly grated horseradish by equal weight for table-condiment use, but jarred products are milder and may contain vinegar, cream or salt; count label salt.
allergen_notes: Dumplings, bread sauces and roux commonly contain wheat and may contain egg or milk. Schnitzel breading contains wheat and egg. Prepared horseradish sauces may contain milk or egg; bouillon and seasoning powders may contain wheat, soy or milk. Nut-filled pastries contain tree nuts and poppy-seed fillings are not a major US allergen. Sesame and peanuts are not defining traditional seasoning allergens.
pitfalls: LOW CONFIDENCE applies to any rule asserted across all five countries. Do not treat paprika as equally dominant in Germany, Austria, Czechia and Poland just because it is central to Hungary. Do not call every meat stew 'goulash': Hungarian gulyás, pörkölt and Austrian/Czech adaptations are distinct. Likewise, dill, caraway and horseradish vary sharply by dish and country.

label: Russian
subtitle: Dill, sourness, horseradish, pickles, rye
about: Russian cuisine developed across an enormous northern Eurasian territory, but this node is best anchored in the historic cooking of European Russia around Moscow, the Volga and northern river systems rather than pretending every cuisine of the Russian Federation is one tradition. Climate, Orthodox fasting, grain agriculture, river fisheries, forest mushrooms and berries, imperial trade and later urban French influence shaped a cuisine rich in soups, porridges, pies, fermentation and oven cooking. Representative dishes include shchi, pelmeni, blini and buckwheat kasha.
sweet_only: vanilla sugar — ванильный сахар (vanilnyy sakhar), mainly baking
cinnamon — корица (koritsa), mainly sweets and hot drinks in modern everyday use, though historical savory use exists
signature_ingredients: tvorog — творог (tvorog) — substitute: farmer cheese or well-drained cottage cheese
smetana — сметана (smetana) — substitute: full-fat sour cream
buckwheat groats — гречка (grechka) — substitute: no close equivalent; use toasted buckwheat/kasha
kvass — квас (kvas) — substitute: none for traditional okroshka; light malt beverage plus acidity is only approximate
salted herring — сельдь (sel'd') — substitute: another mild salted herring
dried porcini — белые грибы (belye griby) — substitute: dried mixed mushrooms plus mushroom powder
techniques: long simmering and gentle oven stewing
salting, drying and preserving mushrooms and fish
shortcuts: Prepared Russian-style mustard can replace another finished mustard 1:1 by weight; formulas range from mild to extremely hot and salt varies by brand.
Prepared horseradish can replace freshly grated horseradish 1:1 by weight as a condiment, but vinegar and salt in jars change the profile; count salt from the label.

Bouillon concentrate can shorten soup preparation but is not equivalent to traditional broth; dilute to package stock strength. Commercial products may contribute substantial salt, calculated from label sodium.
allergen_notes: Smetana and dairy-based sauces contain milk. Blini and many pies contain wheat, egg and often milk. Kvass is commonly made from rye or bread and therefore contains gluten from wheat/rye sources. Mayonnaise-based salads contain egg. Herring, caviar and fish broths contain fish; crayfish-based dishes contain shellfish. Commercial bouillon or seasoning powders may contain wheat or soy. Tree nuts occur in some pastries but are not a defining everyday savory seasoning.
pitfalls: Do not turn every Russian dish into sour cream plus dill, and do not confuse all cuisines of the Russian Federation with ethnic Russian cooking. Fermentation, brine, rye, buckwheat, mushrooms, cabbage and fish are major structural signals. Avoid presenting borscht as exclusively Russian: it is shared across Eastern Europe and is particularly associated with Ukrainian culinary heritage.
sources: Darra Goldstein, The Kingdom of Rye: A Brief History of Russian Food, University of California Press, 2022
Darra Goldstein, A Taste of Russia, Russian Life Books, revised edition 1999
